title: Umamusume anime concerts in U.S. may have to be cancelled over visa problems
description: After six months of trying, organizers say they still don’t have the necessary OK from the U.S. government to bring the horse girl concert to the City of Angels. One of the clearest examples of the surging worldwide popularity of Japanese pop culture is the fact that Umamusume has established a passionate and sizable fanbase […]
content:
After six months of trying, organizers say they still don’t have the necessary OK from the U.S. government to bring the horse girl concert to the City of Angels.

One of the clearest examples of the surging worldwide popularity of Japanese pop culture is the fact that Umamusume has established a passionate and sizable fanbase in the U.S. A sports anime/video game series centered on the souls of real-world Japanese race horses reincarnated as schoolgirls is exactly the sort of thing that used to have no shot at an official overseas release, but the franchise has had so much success in America that two Umamusume concerts are going to be held in Los Angeles this week.

Well, maybe they’re going to be held, because a visa issue could now mean that the performances will have to be cancelled.

Back in June, Umamusume’s 7th Event World Tour: The Stage kicked off with a pair of concerts held at the Ariake Arena in Tokyo. The next stage of the globetrotting event is supposed to be October 22 and 23 at Los Angeles’ Peacock Theater, with 17 Umamusume voice actresses/vocalists scheduled to make the trip across the Pacific to perform.

At 8 p.m. on October 18 (Los Angeles time), though, both the English and Japanese official Umamusume Twitter accounts announced that the concert organizers have still not been able to obtain the required visas for the concert to take place. A statement, posted to the official Umamusume website, says:

“In preparation for the 7th Event: The Stage in Los Angeles concerts planned for Oct 22–23, 2026, we had been working with lawyers and promoters in the US to secure the visas necessary to enter the US since over six months ago, but as of now the visas have yet to be approved.”

Six months seems like it should be plenty of time to process the paperwork for a two-day musical performance, but the United States visa process is notoriously time-consuming in the best of times, and it’s unlikely that the especially chaotic conditions of American bureaucracy these days is making things any easier. That said, while the concerts will only be held for two days, it’s possible that the performers’ talent agencies, since they’re going to the expense of flying so many performers to the U.S., are hoping to have them engage in other promotional activities or professional appearances while in the country, which could be adding complexity to the application process.

Regardless of whether or not six months should be enough time for the U.S. government to have processed the applications, the critical fact is that the concert organizers still don’t have the visas they need, and that’s putting the concerts in jeopardy. A final decision on whether or not to hold the concerts will be made by 10 p.m. on October 19 (Los Angeles time).

Cancelling the concerts would result in some severe headaches for everyone involved, with the matter of refunds being the most immediate problem. Ticket pre-sales for the Los Angeles shows started on July 23, with prices ranging from US$80 all the way up to US$350 for special VIP passes with included merch bundles. Viewing tickets for live-streams of the concerts have also been on sale, priced at US$39 for one day’s performance or US$74 for both, and livestream tickets have even been on sale in Japan for fans who want to watch their favorite voice actresses make their mark on an overseas stage. Then there’s all the concert merchandise that’s scheduled to be offered at the venue, some of which is specific to the Los Angeles performance and would thus be a hard sell if there’s no actual concert happening in the city.

Of course, photo finishes in which victory comes by a split-second margin aren’t uncommon in horse racing, and hopefully all the visa issues can get sorted in time for the concerts to take place as planned, and also that there won’t be any similar problems with the world tour’s next stops in London and Seoul.

Source: Umamusume official website via Anime News Network/Joanna Cayanan, Umamusume 7th Event World Tour: The Stage official website, Twitter/@umamusume_eng, Twitter/@uma_musu

title: Voting begins for Japan’s next top kaiju
description: Which one of these up-and-coming ancient abominations will face off against Godzilla next? The creative minds at Toho have consistently served up a buffet of weird and sometimes wacky creatures known […]
content:
Which one of these up-and-coming ancient abominations will face off against Godzilla next?

Godzilla has had a very long career on the silver screen and has faced countless other giant monsters over the years, from Mothra to Hedorah. The creative minds at Toho have consistently served up a buffet of weird and sometimes wacky creatures known as “kaiju” to satiate moviegoers’ appetites for destruction.

And now, they have decided to let all of us choose a future rival for the King of All Monsters in the New Kaiju General Election. This online vote has pitted eight forces of nature, cosmic entities, and man-made golems in a contest of popularity now entering its final phase.

From 17 to 25 October, Phase 2 of the final voting will be held. The previous phase saw the top four finalists go head to spiky head with the following results.

1st Place
Dimensional Entity
Xenolhu
(46,066 points, 58 meters [190.3 feet] tall, 45,000 metric tonnes [49,604 tons])

This octopus-like monstrosity hails from another universe. When Godzilla’s heat ray emitted wavelengths similar to those harnessed by Xenolhu, it came to Earth to learn more and attempt to wipe out existence while it’s here. This bad boy can grab and manipulate space as if it were matter and has telepathic powers that can cause hallucinations or reduce living beings to ash.

2nd Place
Drone Carrier Machine
Sagius
(34,202 points, 60 meters tall, 35,000 tonnes)

Drones are all the rage in warfare these days, and Sagius has them in spades. In fact, the whole thing is a man-made drone aircraft carrier designed with the sole purpose of fighting Godzilla. Its hind legs that cause it to resemble Sagittarius also provide it with incredible stability in case the big green guy does that weird move where he comes flying horizontally at it. It can also utilize its dreaded Maser Arrow, in which its powerful Maser Cannon in its midsection fires a massive maser beam that’s amplified by a constellation of maser drones around it… and don’t ask me what “maser” means. I just like saying it.

3rd Place
Planet Raid Monster
Glix
(28,724 points, 70 meters tall, 40,000 tonnes and up)

Here we have one of those planet-devouring monsters that travels through space looking for energy-rich worlds to consume and, according to its English bio, “reduce planets to ‘Dead Stars,’” reminding us all about the importance of using human translators. Glix could smell the smoldering radioactive power inside Godzilla from light-years away and came to dine on Godzilla while also reducing the Earth to a dead, sigh… star…

It’s just, setting aside the fact that planets and stars are vastly different things, actual dead stars like white dwarves and black holes still have staggering amounts of energy in them. Anyway…

4th Place
Assault Dinosaur Monster
Rigedoh
(18,846 points, 50 meters tall, 32,000 tonnes)

Rigedoh is a really big dinosaur that was frozen in the ice for eons.

That’s it really…

What? It’s not like all these monsters have to have complex backstories. Some are just cool-looking dinosaurs. and if you can’t find joy in that while watching Godzilla movies, then you have come to the wrong place, my friend.

As you can see by the point spread, Xenolhu has a very commanding lead so far, but there’s nothing kaiju love more than crunch time, and this is it! All you have to do is go to the official voting website, read through the monsters’ bios and check out their concept art, and then vote for your favorite.

▼ You can also check out the ones that didn’t make the finals: (from top left clockwise) Gigasect, the giant insectoid, the eldritch Madomuh, Candyroy (who started out as a mutated candy wrapper and did abysmally in the vote), and the ancient mech Minacias.

Voting closes on 25 October, and the winner will be crowned the New Kaiju on 3 November at Godzilla Fest 2026 at the Takanawa Gateway Convention Center in Tokyo. This winning beast or mech will then feature in a special battle short film screened at the following year’s Godzilla Fest in the tokusatsu style of the campier Godzilla films, as opposed to the more current darker ones. 

It may not be a feature film, but this is still a major stepping stone for any aspiring colossus that could lead to further TV and film appearances, and dare I say maybe even an unposable plastic toy in the future. The producers at Toho will also be keeping their eyes on all contestants, and even those who don’t come in first may get tapped for a future project if they get enough support. That’s why it’s important to get out there and vote for your favorite kaiju. After all, democracy is the backbone of monster mayhem.

title: Eight low-key great places to spend the day (or half a day) in Japan this fall
description: Fall means an abundance of good weather but a shortage of time in Japan, but here are eight spots that are quick to see but you’ll remember for a long, long time. There’s a strong case to be made that autumn is the most comfortable time of year for going out in Japan. The summer […]
content:
Fall means an abundance of good weather but a shortage of time in Japan, but here are eight spots that are quick to see but you’ll remember for a long, long time.

There’s a strong case to be made that autumn is the most comfortable time of year for going out in Japan. The summer heat, humidity, and thunderstorms are all done, but the cold weather and short daylight hours of winter haven’t set in yet. The cruel irony, though, is that Japan’s three vacation seasons, New Year’s, Golden Week, and Obon, take place in the winter, spring, and summer. Autumn has a few scattered holidays, but extended time off from work or school are hard to come by at this time of year.

So what we need is a selection of great places to spend half a day or so in autumn, and to put a list together we turned to a number of our writers. Let’s take a look at their recommendations of places they’ve visited that turned out to be low-key awesome.

● Hakone Open-Air Museum
Website

The town of Hakone, in the mountains of Kanagawa Prefecture, is most famous for its hot spring baths and lake cruises with views of Mt. Fuji. But if you can carve out time in your schedule for the Open-Air Museum, which has both indoor and outdoor sculptures on display, including many pieces by Picaso, you won’t be disappointed (and yes, the museum has a hot spring foot bath too).

We just sort of stumbled into the place on a family trip, but we ended up having a great time. It feels more like a park than a museum, and there’s plenty of space for kids to move around. I’m not even that much of an art lover usually, but we were there for three hours, and I never felt bored. – P.K. Sanjun

● Attack on Titan in Hita Museum
Website

Sort of like Hakone, Oita Prefecture, which the town of Hita is part of, is primarily famous for its hot springs, and once again we’ve got a unique museum experience. Hita is the hometown of Hajime Isayama, the manga artist and creator of the smash-hit series, and the city’s museum houses a collection of original Attack on Titan artwork donated by Isayama, as well as the work desk at which he drew during the series’ serialization.

I was kind of surprised that the museum has a whole exhibit of Attack on Titan stuff, and was really impressed by how extensive it is. Obviously it’s great for hardcore otaku, but it’s cool even for people who are more casual fans, and combining a visit to the museum with seeing some of the fall leaves in the town shows that thee’s more than hot spring to Oita’s appeal. – Takashi Harada

● Dragon Maze
Website

It’s hard to say what the most impressive thing is about this maze in the hills of Unnan, Shimane Prefecture. Its massive size? The fact that it’s built by hand? The way it keeps getting bigger because the owner keeps adding on to it, based on visions he has in his dreams? Really, there’s no other place in Japan quite like the Dragon Maze.

I think almost all of the giant mazes like this that you used to be able to find in Japan are gone now, but this one in Unnan is a survivor. It first opened in 1987 and then closed down in 1999, but it was relocated and reopened in 2007. Every year since then the maze has gotten bigger and more and more people have come to try it, turning it into a beloved local amusement attraction.

The whole thing is hand-built, but it’s so complex that’s it’s a serious challenge even for adults. I’d actually wonder if little kids can find their way all the way through to the goal? When it first reopened, the maze had a total area of about 1,000 hectares, but by 2022 it had grown to seven times that size. At this pace, it’ll be 10,000 hectares before long.
– Mr. Sato

● Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building
Website

The Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building, a.k.a. Tocho, is essentially Tokyo’s city hall, but there are plenty of reasons to go there besides taking care of local government paperwork. Each of its towers boasts an observation floor at the top with panoramic views of Tokyo and even Mt. Fuji, and it’s even a great place to grab a bite to eat.

For years, I’ve been dropping by here when I’ve got spare time. Both of the observation floors are free to go up to, and the view from each is slightly different. Once you’ve had you fill of that, you can head to the cafeteria. It’s the same one used by workers in the building, so the prices are really reasonable, and there’s a neat inside vibe to it. You can get drinks and snacks in the observation floor too, and I like having something to sip or munch on while watching the sunset. Once it’s nighttime, they also sometimes have projection mapping shows on the outside of the building, so there’s something cool to see even after you come back down to street level. – Go Hatori

● Arakawa Amusement Park
Website

You don’t need to go all the way out to Disneyland for a day at an amusement park in the Tokyo area! Known as Arakawa Yuen in Japanese, this old-school amusement is located in a suburban part of Tokyo’s Arakawa Ward, along the bank of the Sumida River.

This place is a hidden gem, and a lot less crowded and touristy than other amusement parks. The Ferris wheel is really nice, but my personal favorite attraction is the Sky Cycle, where you ride pedal cars on an elevated track that goes around the park. It’s surprisingly fun to feel like you’re biking through the sky! They also have special events, like the zoo event when I went with my kids last summer and we took that picture with the sloth.

The biggest surprise though is how reasonably priced this place is. Admission and unlimited rides is just 1,800 yen (US$11.30) for adults, 1,000 yen for junior high students, and 700 yen for elementary school-age kids! There’s enough stuff to do here to spend the whole day in the park, so it’s a great deal, and they even have discounted tickets for entry after 4 in the afternoon. The place looks really pretty when it’s lit up at night too, so it’s seriously tough to beat. – Yoshio

● Small Worlds
Website

Not to be confused with the Disneyland attraction of a very similar name, Small Worlds is a unique miniature art exhibition facility in Tokyo’s Ariake island neighborhood in Tokyo Bay. Each area has huge, intricately detailed dioramas of cityscapes both real and imagined, including the Tokyo-3 anime metropolis from Evangelion.

I came to this miniatures museum to see the Evangelion exhibits, but the other areas, like the space center, airport, and whimsical European-style village, were all way more detailed than I’d expected and drew me into their little worlds. Each one of them has a massively convincing sense of place.

The adult admission price is pretty high at 3,200 yen, so I wasn’t sure how much I was going to enjoy this place, but there was so much cool stuff to see that I was totally satisfied. Eva fans especially will have a blast here, but I think it’d be a fun visit for anybody.
– Takamichi Furusawa

● Imperial Palace Outer Gardens
Website

Also known as the Kokyo Gaien National Garden, this outer layer of the grounds of the Imperial Palace in Tokyo requires no ticket to get into, and the park-like atmosphere, but without the crowds of more famous downtown green spaces like Ueno Park, earn it a place on our list.

I don’t think there’s a better “if you know, you know” place in Tokyo than this. It’s located just a couple of blocks from Tokyo Station, but the atmosphere is so laidback and relaxing, a little peaceful oasis so close to one of the busiest places in the city that a lot of people forget it’s there. There’s a lot of historical significance to the place too, and it’s fun just to walk around, and it’s perfect for an autumn afternoon with good weather. – Yuichiro Wasai

● Hitachi Seaside Park
Website

Located in the coastal town of Hitachinaka in Ibaraki Prefecture, this sprawling park is a nice in spring and summer too, but if you can plan for an autumn visit, you’ll be glad you did. That’s when the park’s hills of kochia shrubs turn a dramatic shade of crimson, becoming an utterly unforgettable and unique addition to Japan’s fall-color scenery.

Ibraraki might be two prefecture away from Tokyo, but if you time your train and bus transfers right, you can get from the capital to Hitachi Seaside Park in about an hour and a half. The park is huge, with forested areas, bicycling paths, and reconstructed farm houses, but nothing compares to the surreal impact of seeing the kochia in fall. The hills aren’t very steep, but they’re high enough that once you get to the top you’re rewarded with a view of the sea of red from a different perspective, so make sure to make the walk up. – Casey Baseel

title: Tokyo bakery has a crazy expensive 10,000-yen bread loaf set, and we’ve tried it [Taste test]
description: Japan’s luxury bread loaf boom was supposed to have died down, but apparently no one told this Ginza bakery. A couple of years ago, premium-priced loaves of bread were all the rage among foodies in Japan. Luxury bakeries sprang up one after another, with long lines of customers waiting to get in and drop 1,000 […]
content:
Japan’s luxury bread loaf boom was supposed to have died down, but apparently no one told this Ginza bakery.

A couple of years ago, premium-priced loaves of bread were all the rage among foodies in Japan. Luxury bakeries sprang up one after another, with long lines of customers waiting to get in and drop 1,000 yen (US$6;30) or so on a single loaf, several times more than what you’d pay for the same quantity at a supermarket.

As is often the case, though, after a while the fad faded, and pricy bakeries began to gradually disappear and be replaced by new tenants chasing the next foodie trend. One of the survivors of the luxury bread loaf glory days, though, is Ginza Nishikawa.

▼ Ginza Nishikawa’s flagship branch in Ginza

With half of its name coming from Tokyo’s fashionable and wealthy Ginza neighborhood, you’d be correct in assuming that the bakery chain hasn’t abandoned its high-quality, high-cost philosophy regarding its baked goods. While many other purveyors of 1,000-yen loaves of bread have had to fold up shop, Ginza Nishikawa has recently begun offering a bread loaf set, which it calls Shigoku (“The Supreme”), with an eye-watering price of 10,000 yen (US$63)!

This quickly caught the attention of our Japanese-language reporter P.K. Sanjun. However, while P.K. and his stomach were in agreement that he should definitely try the Shigoku for himself, his wallet had a firmly dissenting opinion on the matter. Luckily for P.K., this deadlock was resolved, or rather rendered irrelevant, when he was able to snag an invitation to a tasting event for the 10,000-yen set held at Ginza Nishikawa’s Ginza branch, which is the exclusive location offering the Shigoku.

Upon arrival, P.K. learned that the Shigoku is a set of two loaves of bread, meaning that they’re essentially 5,000 yen each. This still makes them the most expensive loaves of bread that he’s ever tasted, though.

Why are they so expensive? Because of the ingredients Ginza Nishikawa uses. The first of the two loaves is the Kumamoto Yamaeguri Bread, made with chestnuts from Kumamoto Prefecture, and the other is a loaf of Hand-churned Cultured Butter Croissant Bread.

P.K. tasted slices from each loaf both as-is and toasted. Starting with the Kumamoto chestnut loaf, P.K.’s initial reaction was that more so than bread, it feels like some kind of midway point between a loaf of bread and a poundcake, but closer to the latter.

This is, of course, not a complaint. There’s a very generous portion of chestnuts in every possible slice, and with whipped cream mixed into the batter before baking, the bread itself is rich, moist, and delicious.

The similarities with cake, though, make for kind of an unnatural sensation when eating the Kumamoto chestnut bread as toast, so P.K. recommends just slicing off a piece to eat without any extra cooking or crisping.

On the other hand, the hand-churned cultured butter loaf feels 100-percent like bread.

Sure, there’s a very smooth richness coming from the butter, which is produced by Yamanaka Dairy Farm in Hokkaido, Japan’s premiere prefecture for dairy products. But whereas the Kumamoto chestnut bread feels like a sweet snack or dessert, the hand-churned butter loaf still works best if used like normal bread, which means its toasts up very nicely too.

So in the end, is the supreme Shigoku set worth what Ginza Nishikawa is asks for it? It’s a tricky question to answer, since 10,000 yen is so far beyond the normal price point for bread that it messes with the sense of psychological scale to try to weight whether this, say, 20, 30, or 40 times more satisfying than a regular loaf of bread. On the other hand, if someone were going to spend 10,000 yen on bread, P.K. thinks this would be a fine, very tasty way to do so.

As you can probably imagine, Ginza Nishikawa doesn’t just bake up a bunch of Shigoku loaves every morning and set them out on the shelves in case someone wants to buy a set. Instead, you have to order the set ahead of time, with at least five days’ advance notice required. A total of 1,000 sets will be offered between October 20 and December 25, and reservations can be made online here.

title: New Studio Ghibli stamps – Too cute to wait until New Year’s to use, so they’re available right now
description: Totoro and the Catbus are ready to help you get started on wishing for good luck and happiness even before we get to nengajo season. Japan doesn’t really do Christmas cards, but the country does have a custom of New Year’s cards, or nengajo, as they’re called in Japanese. The end of the year tends […]
content:
Totoro and the Catbus are ready to help you get started on wishing for good luck and happiness even before we get to nengajo season.

Japan doesn’t really do Christmas cards, but the country does have a custom of New Year’s cards, or nengajo, as they’re called in Japanese. The end of the year tends to be an especially busy time, though, especially since the end of December/start of January is a vacation period in Japan, meaning people are often scrambling to wrap up work or school projects.

So for anyone who needs a hand getting their New Year’s cards looking extra-nice, there’s a very helpful assistant on the way: Totoro!

Studio Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku has just released its lineup of nengajo stamps for this year, with four different designs featuring adorable My Neighbor Totoro artwork. Pictured above is the big forest spirit himself, playing his ocarina while his Small Totoro counterpart is perched on his head and one of Japan’s phrases for “Happy New Year” appears written in kanji characters.

▼ The phrase geishun, used in written greetings, is made with the kajnji for “welcoming” (迎) and “spring” (春), harkening back to classical Japanese seasonal concepts in which spring was considered to start soon after the new year.

Of course, you don’t have to use this stamp exclusively for New Year’s cards. Put a little scrap of paper or some other sort of cover on the part of your inkpad where the contours of the kanji would come into contact with the ink, and you could stamp just the Totoros anywhere you’d like.

Similarly, while this stamp with the Small Totoro riding a ram, the Chinese Zodiac animal for 2027 (which Japan starts recognizing from January 1), will still be cute year-round, and could also work as a decorative accent at the lunar New Year

The Soot Sprite design, with a stylized Catbus too, sports an array of traditional Japanese good-luck items (a fan, top, and gourd), which are especially appropriate at New Year’s, but wouldn’t be out of place on any note or letter you’re giving to someone who you’re wishing good fortune on.

And last, the Catbus solo stamp has the famous feline dashing towards Omedetou gozaimasu, a version of “Happy New Year” for both spoken conversation and written correspondence, rendered all in phonetic hiragana script, making it a fun message that should be easy to read for any acquaintances who’re starting their journey towards Japanese proficiency.

The Small Totoro/ram and Soot Sprite/Catbus stamps are priced at 792 yen (US$5) each, the Catbus solo stamp 1,265 yen, and the Big Totoro/Small Totoro design 1,540 yen. They’re all available through the Donguri Kyowakoku online store here right now for anyone who’s getting a very early start on their New Year’s Cards, or for anyone who needs Totoro’s help with some other arts and crafts projects right now.

title: The cheapest bento at this Osaka shop is only 200 yen, but is it actually any good?
description: Does the taste match its simple appearance? Being too busy, lacking energy, the store having a fantastic campaign going on, or having the last time you set foot in the kitchen being known as “the day the frying pan begged for mercy”…there are a multitude of reasons why you would pick up a meal to-go […]
content:
Does the taste match its simple appearance?

Being too busy, lacking energy, the store having a fantastic campaign going on, or having the last time you set foot in the kitchen being known as “the day the frying pan begged for mercy”…there are a multitude of reasons why you would pick up a meal to-go from a nearby store. For students in particular, these ready-to-eat meals can be a lifesaver, so when there’s also an option that comes in at a low price point, it could very well be anointed as a divine blessing.

Our Japanese-language reporter Seiji Nakazawa has long been a fan of takeout bento, but prices have risen considerably since his days as a sprightly young lad. He used to be able to regularly find simple, no-frills boxed lunches for as little as 300 yen (US$1.89), but now even the cheapest options at many major chains start above 500. So when Seiji heard there exists a store selling a 200-yen bento, off he went to pay a visit to the ultra-budget bento shop known as Sandaime Kacchan in Osaka.

Seiji strolled through the Kyobashi Chuo Shopping District, also known as Rib Street, and about a five-minute walk north of both JR and Keihan Kyobashi Stations (and a couple more minutes from Kyobashi Station on the Nagahoritsurumiryokuchi Subway Line) he soon spotted the store front’s sign with a menu of its products displayed outside.

Perusing the bento for sale, Seiji was impressed with how many different varieties come in under the cheapest boxed lunches available at major chains. Seiji noticed that Sandaime Kacchan’s menu also includes a statement about how the store has been featured on television as “Osaka’s cheapest bento shop,” so now he was really keen to try it out.

As if the menu wasn’t indication enough of Sandaime Kacchan’s low prices, they have also pasted an announcement of the rumored “200-yen bento” on the glass next to the entrance, so any visitor will know they have come to the right place.

Entering inside, Seiji took in the scene of various bento lined up before him, with his 200-yen bento goal on the far left, and the options increasing in price the further right they’re placed. Seiji picked up on the fact that the “200 yen” claim was accurate, although it indicates the pre-tax price, so a customer would actually be handing over 216 yen to dine on the store’s offerings.

Scanning over the rest of the bento, they all looked pretty appetizing, such as the pork fillet cutlet bento (432 yen), grilled fish bento (486 yen), and special hamburger steak bento (540 yen). The most expensive item in the store was the Mega Serving DX Hamburger Steak Set for 842 yen, containing a hamburger steak and two fried shrimp, which looked like it would be a great deal.

The other customers in the store came in, picked up various bento, and appeared to leave happily, but Seiji was here for one reason: the 200-yen bento, so, here it is.

Rice with chinjao rosu (Japanese-style pepper steak made with pork and green peppers), macaroni salad, and pink pickled radish. The lack of volume and color in the ensemble was very much evocative of its price of 216 yen, especially when compared to its more impressive-looking siblings being sold alongside it.

However, when Seiji took a bite, he was struck by how delicious it was. A sweet and savory taste with a sharp, spicy kick that went well with the peppers and meat. Considering that the bento cost 216 yen to begin with, Seiji was simply impressed by the fact that the chinjao rosu actually contained meat to begin with.

Despite its lackluster looks, the bento did not taste like a 216-yen meal. It tasted far beyond that. In fact, there were some among the customers that Seiji saw that bought it as an add-on item for something like the pork fillet cutlet bento, and seeing as how the two items together costs 648 yen, it now seemed like a really smart option to get a delicious and filling meal for a low cost. Combining this with the atmosphere of the shopping district where Sandaime Kacchan is located, which Seiji thought felt like a run-down back alley, he feels that just from this little outing alone he got a taste of whole other side of Osaka’s food culture.

title: Man in Suzuka offered 9 million yen for his semen, conned out of 38 million yen
description: It was just too good to be true. Despite constant efforts by police and government organizations in Japan, the wave of “special fraud” (tokushu sagi) seems to continue unabated. And as the years go by, the tactics employed by these thieves seem to constantly evolve from pretending to be an elderly person’s son to pretending […]
content:
It was just too good to be true.

Despite constant efforts by police and government organizations in Japan, the wave of “special fraud” (tokushu sagi) seems to continue unabated. And as the years go by, the tactics employed by these thieves seem to constantly evolve from pretending to be an elderly person’s son to pretending to be Mick Jagger or an astronaut in orbit.

One would think the more outlandish these premises get, the less likely they are to succeed, but they do time and time again. Just take a look at the case of a man in his 70s living in the city of Suzuka, Mie Prefecture, who was taken in by an extravagant offer for his sperm.

According to an investigation by the Mie Prefectural Police, the victim met “a woman” online and last April she sent a message over social media, offering nine million yen (US$57,000) if he provided her with his semen.

After a tentative deal was reached, the woman put the man in contact with “her lawyers” to set the terms and finalize the deal. From this point on, the woman’s legal team continuously requested payments from the man for things such as a non-disclosure agreement and to unfreeze a bank account. The man was instructed to do so by purchasing prepaid electronic currency cards.

▼ People claiming to be police or lawyers while asking for something like WebMoney cards is one of the bigger red flags of these scams.

Nearly 600 prepaid cards and about 38 million yen ($240,000) in payments later, the man suspected something was wrong and consulted an actual lawyer. The attorney recognized this as a case of special fraud and advised the man to go to the police, who are currently investigating the matter.

They say the crime was accomplished in a manner similar to a romance scam, where a strong relationship is built up over a long time before the actual fraud begins. They didn’t explain how this situation played out, since that would essentially be teaching us all how to commit a crime, but it really must have been a truly elaborate ploy to convince someone they could sell their semen.

Online comments were also baffled by how things could have gotten to the point they did.

“To think you could swindle 38 million with something like that. I guess anything can be used for a scam.”
“How could anyone fall for that?”
“Yeah, I’ll give you 9 million, but you’ll have to give me 38 million first…”
“The fact that he had 38 million to give would suggest he wasn’t even doing it for the money.”
“At least no one got hurt.”
“Who’d want a 70-year-old’s sperm even for free?”
“And you know they’re never going to catch these people.”
“He’s either suffering from dementia or a dimwit.”

It’s easy to write this victim off as merely being slow on the uptake, but the facts would suggest otherwise.

This elderly person somehow managed to purchase 571 prepaid cards from various convenience stores over months without arousing the suspicion of staff, who are now trained to identify and stop potential fraud victims, epitomized by a senior citizen buying e-currency cards. Sure, he could have slipped by lazy clerks once or twice, but he would definitely need to have his wits about him and then some to pull off buying that many cards.

Even in general, it’s dangerous to assume these victims are merely foolish, because it underestimates the scammers’ ability to operate on an emotional level, creating a fog that blinds people to conventional logic. That kind of dismissive thinking just makes it easier for them to sneak in and exploit people’s feelings of love, fear, or loneliness.

Perhaps that’s why these crimes continue in the face of all the informational awareness-raising campaigns going on in Japan. They may never go away until everyone remembers that it’s just as important to be emotionally stable as it is to be aware.

title: Burger King Japan now selling hamburgers minus everything but the meat
description: On the Beef is back, but in a sense it never really left. Burger King Japan has made a linguistically confusing addition to its menu, and it’s one that’s culinarily puzzling too. Yes, even more so than the Pickleball Burgers we looked at earlier this month. The just-added item is called On the Beef. As […]
content:
On the Beef is back, but in a sense it never really left.

Burger King Japan has made a linguistically confusing addition to its menu, and it’s one that’s culinarily puzzling too. Yes, even more so than the Pickleball Burgers we looked at earlier this month.

The just-added item is called On the Beef. As we’ve previously discussed, though, you can’t eat a grammatical preposition, and while the name “On the Beef” would have one expecting some undetermined additional element being placed on beef, the On the Beef is just beef.

I suppose you could argue that because it’s prepared with a dash of salt and pepper, there technically are some granulated seasonings on the On the Beef. That still doesn’t change the fact, though, that Burger King is selling a hamburger patty for 450 yen (US$2.85), leaving out the bun, lettuce, and anything else that would be included in a burger, the very thing that Burger King claims royal dominion over. This isn’t a special, high-grade patty made of a premium breed of wagyu beef, either. It’s the same patty that Burger King uses for its actual sandwiches, with the chain saying the point of the On the Beef is to be a way for customers to get a taste of the all-beef patties that go into the chain’s sandwiches.

So spartan is the On the Beef that the regular version doesn’t include ketchup or any other sort of sauce. You can ask for a squirt of spicy tomato jalapeno, smokey barbecue, or teriyaki sauce, but there’s an additional fee, since the Sauce on the Beef, as it’s called, will cost you 550 yen.

Alternatively, the Beef on the Beef, two patties with salt and pepper, can be yours for 900 yen…

…and finally there’s the top-of-the-line Sauce on the Double Beef (which seems like it should be called the Sauce on the Beef on the Beef), two patties with sauce, for 1,000 yen.

The On the Beef has become a sort of irregular autumn tradition at Burger King Japan, and while the concept seems baffling for a burger joint, it makes a little more sense within the broader context of the Japanese food industry. Hamburger steaks are popular in Japan. People eat them with assorted vegetables and rice or bread on the side, as part of bento boxed lunches, or as a topping for curry rice. Because of that, the idea of “Hey, a patty should have a bun!” isn’t as entrenched in Japan as it is iin the U.S., and you can find pre-made, ready-to-eat hamburger steaks for sale at grocery stores.

That being said, there’s a difference between shopping at a supermarket, where people buy ingredients, and walking into a fast food restaurant, where most people are looking for a whole meal, especially since Burger King doesn’t sell rice, curry, or any of the other things one might use to build a meal around a hamburger steak, so you’ll have to prepare any desired accompaniments on your own, like we did.

In terms of price, the On the Beef is actually more expensive than the most affordable hamburger that Burger King Japan offers, its 360-yen cheeseburger. However, the On the Beef looks to use the same patty as the larger Whopper, which starts at 690 yen, so you’re saving 240 yen by jettisoning everything from the sandwich but the meat.

▼ And you get a sticker for ordering the On the Beef (while supplies last).

The On the Beef made its return on October 16, and will be on sale until October 22, though you could make the argument that really it’ll still be available after that date as long as you’re willing to pull the patty out of a Burger King hamburger yourself.

title: Osaka’s famous Glico Running Man will be removed and replaced with a new-look sign
description: Now’s the time to say goodbye to the city’s sixth running man before he disappears forever.  If you’ve ever been to Osaka, one of the landmarks you’ve probably taken a photo in front of is the Glico “running man” sign. While this might sound like an odd tourist draw, the giant signboard has become one […]
content:
Now’s the time to say goodbye to the city’s sixth running man before he disappears forever. 

If you’ve ever been to Osaka, one of the landmarks you’ve probably taken a photo in front of is the Glico “running man” sign. While this might sound like an odd tourist draw, the giant signboard has become one of the most famous sites in the prefecture, with the arms-raised athlete connecting with visitors from around the globe, who may or may not be aware that the sign is actually an ad for one of the country’s most popular confectionery makers.

▼ The sign reportedly attracts an estimated 70,000 to 80,000 visitors a day.

The signboard is so famous that when its operators, Ezaki Glico, announced that it would be disappearing from the landscape for several months for a makeover, it became a national news story. Glico made the announcement at a press conference in Osaka on 14 October, where it revealed that the current Glico running man sign – the sixth of its kind, which has been overlooking the river since 2014 – will be replaced by a seventh-generation version next spring.

▼ Sayonara, number six.

That means the current running man’s days are numbered, with Glico saying that work on the signboard will commence in December. As for what the new design will look like, well, Glico is keeping that a secret, but company representative Yoriko Miki told reporters that the runner will remain the main attraction. According to Miki, the running man represents the company’s founding spirit and its purpose of helping people enjoy “Healthy days, a fulfilling life”.

▼ グリコ = Glico

The company has long held close ties with Osaka, having been founded there 104 years ago, in 1922. The signboard has enjoyed a similarly long history, appearing beside Ebisubashi Bridge in 1935, where it towered over the landscape at a height of 33 metres (108 feet), with large neon lettering making it stand out at night.

▼ It quickly became a local landmark, but was dismantled in 1943 as materials were needed for the war.

Then, from 1955 to 1963, the second incarnation took up residence in the same location, this time above a stage with a giant toy crocodile playing the piano.

From 1963 to 1972, things got even wilder, with the third sign featuring an elaborate fountain that sprayed 12 tonnes of water from 150 nozzles arranged around the runner, illuminated by hundreds of coloured lights to create a colourful effect.

The fourth sign, in place from 1972 to 1996, included a version of the running track we now see today, but after it was switched off and removed due to renovation work on the neighbouring building, Osaka was without its running man for a whole year.

For the fifth iteration, which ran from 1998 to 2014, the colours of the background changed to simulate the passage of a whole day, making it look as if the runner was racing through Osaka from morning until night.

The current, sixth-generation sign continues the running man tradition of being lit up over the river, with around 140,000 LED lights illuminating him through the night.

▼ The backgrounds also changed to show the runner travelling through locations in Japan and around the world.

In looking back at the history of the sign itself, it’s interesting to see just how many forms it’s taken over the years, all while remaining a beloved symbol of the region. As for whether the seventh iteration will be equally welcomed, or reviled like the Suica successors in Tokyo, we’ll have to wait until March 2027 to find out. For now, you’ll want to make your way to Dotonbori to say your farewells, and let anyone who’s visiting Osaka know that the running man won’t be running this winter.

title: Japanese taxi drivers granted right to kick rude passengers out of their cabs before destination
description: If passengers can’t be polite, then they can be walking. Earlier this year we took a look at a change in the rules regarding taxis in Japan when the government gave the OK for ultracompact kei cars to start being used as cabs. Now comes another revision to regulations aimed at keeping the taxi experience […]
content:
If passengers can’t be polite, then they can be walking.

Earlier this year we took a look at a change in the rules regarding taxis in Japan when the government gave the OK for ultracompact kei cars to start being used as cabs. Now comes another revision to regulations aimed at keeping the taxi experience civil by giving drivers the right to kick passengers out of their cabs if they can’t behave themselves.

Up until now, taxi drivers in Japan have only been allowed to pull over and tell a passenger to get out of the vehicle under pretty specific conditions, such as the customer becoming physically violent, being in possession of illegal or dangerous items, or being too intoxicated to intelligently verbalize their desired destination. The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism has now disclosed that it is making amendments to the Standard Terms and Conditions of Carriage, the underlying rules of the taxi industry, which will explicitly give drivers the right to order passengers out of their cab for being verbally abusive, making unreasonable demands, or engaging in otherwise disruptive behavior. The same rights will also be granted to bus drivers.

This expansion of drivers’ authority comes in the wake of another regulatory change which went into effect at the star of this month, requiring taxi and bus operators to put in place protocols by which to protect drivers from harassment by customers. Since requiring a driver to continue carrying problematic passengers would constitute exposing them to such harassment, the logical solution is to give drivers the power to remove rude jerks, even if it means they’ll have to walk home from wherever their ride came to an abrupt end.

The question of what to do if a belligerent passenger then becomes defiant too and refuses to vacate the vehicle appears to be something that individual operators will need to establish protocols for, but ostensibly contacting the police are having them remove the passenger, in the same way that trespassers within private property are dealt with, would be an option.

The new regulation is expected to go into effect before the end of the year, so anyone who’s gotten into the habit of throwing their weight around when they hop in a taxi would be advised to polish their manners sooner rather than later.

title: This Japanese sandwich mascot is filled with fiery rage, and he’s got a point [Video]
description: Pocket sandwich innovator is sick and tired of being called an imitation, and furious too. Npa might not be Japan’s most famous mascot character, perhaps because of his difficult-to-pronounce name, but you can’t really fault his design. Not only is the spokescharacter for Fuji Baking cute, he’s also an anthropomorphized version of the company’s pocket […]
content:
Pocket sandwich innovator is sick and tired of being called an imitation, and furious too.

Npa might not be Japan’s most famous mascot character, perhaps because of his difficult-to-pronounce name, but you can’t really fault his design. Not only is the spokescharacter for Fuji Baking cute, he’s also an anthropomorphized version of the company’s pocket sandwiches, which it calls Snack Sandwiches.

Like most Japanese mascot characters, Npa is usually shown to have a friendly, earnest, and unassuming personality. We see that agreeable aura on display in a recent promotional video from Fuji Baking that depicts Npa as an office worker at the company. Sure, he may end up spewing egg salad into an elevator filled with his coworkers, but that was an honest accident.

Even when he’s sitting at his desk and looking at social media, it’s all in the name of market research to see how people are enjoying the different varieties of Snack Sandwich that are currently on the market.

This might be your first time hearing about Snack Sandwich, but if you’re the sort of well-cultured scholar who regularly reads SoraNews24, this probably isn’t your first time hearing about Japan’s pocket sandwiches. Fuji Baking competitor Yamazaki Baking’s Lunch Pack series is far and away the most prevalent and popular brand of pocket sandwiches in Japan, so much so that “Lunch Pack” has become practically a generic term for the sandwich type, and we ourselves often eat Lunch Packs for both personal and professional taste-testing reasons.

Lunch Pack is so ubiquitous, and has been around for so long (since 1984), that many people assume that the brand was the originator of pocket sandwiches in Japan, and with Npa not making his debut until 2016, a lot of people also assume that Snack Sandwich is one of a number of Lunch Pack imitators.

But wait a second let’s take another look at the Snack Sandwich packaging, which says…“since 1975?” And that’s not all — it also says ganso (元祖), which means “the original.”

Yes, not only are people incorrect in thinking that Snack Sandwich is a Lunch Pack imitator, every other company that they also think is imitating Lunch Pack, as well as Lunch Pack itself, is actually imitating Snack Sandwich, since it was the first to hit store shelves.

However, in a survey 87 percent of people said that they didn’t think that Snack Sandwich was Japan’s original pocket sandwich brand, and it definitely has less cachet than Lunch Pack does. So in the video, as Npa continues scrolling through online posts, he comes across ones such as “Ah, woops! I messed up and bought Snack Sandwich by mistake” and “Agh, I screwed up! Bought that lookalike Fuji Baking one instead.”

He…doesn’t take this well.

“Even though it’s the original,” screams the narrator, “87 percent of people think it’s not!” So great is Npa’s rage over this injustice that he grows to gargantuan kaiju-class size, bursting through the walls of Fuji Baking’s headquarters and firing beams of fiery indignation as he rampages across the city.

▼ “Take back the title of the original! Npa Strikes Back!”

In hindsight, the video’s narrator was a clue that things were going to go off the rails, as its provided by veteran anime voice actor Shigeru Chiba, whose credits include such less-than-even-tempered individuals as both Kefka and Profssor Hojo from the Final Fantasy franchise, Patlabor’s Shigeo Shiba, and One Piece’s Buggy.

OK, but now that Npa has blown off some steam, the frustration is out of his system, right?

Apparently not.

▼ “He will rage until 100 percent of the people know.”

In the month since the video was posted, it’s been viewed an astounding 13.69 million times, so no doubt more people know about Snack Sandwich’s pioneering status now than they did before. And Npa does seem to have calmed down enough that he looks to be back to having carefree fun on the packages for Snack Sandwich’s Halloween lineup of chestnut, apple, purple potato, and pumpkin cream fillings.

None of his Halloween costumes look particularly scary, but that’s probably just because no outfit could make him look as terrifying as his burning anger can.

title: Studio Ghibli creates illustrated Kyoto sightseeing map, available at any 7-Eleven Japan store
description: Zen and Ghibli map also makes for a beautiful mini poster. Unlike most other major cities in Japan, Kyoto doesn’t have a dense network of train and subway lines crisscrossing it. Rail options are pretty limited within the city, and with buses often filled to capacity, it’s not unusual to find yourself in a situation […]
content:
Zen and Ghibli map also makes for a beautiful mini poster.

Unlike most other major cities in Japan, Kyoto doesn’t have a dense network of train and subway lines crisscrossing it. Rail options are pretty limited within the city, and with buses often filled to capacity, it’s not unusual to find yourself in a situation where walking to the next spot on your travel itinerary could be the best option, especially since Kyoto has so many historically significant sites that it might not be all that long a trek.

Of course, navigating the streets of Kyoto becomes much easier with a map, and it becomes both easier and awesome if it’s an illustrated map produced by Studio Ghibli.

Produced as a companion to the Zen and Ghibli art/cultural exhibition currently being held at the Kyoto City Kyocera Museum of Art, the Kyoto Zen Guide Presented by Zen and Ghibli, also known as the just the Zen Map for short, gives anime fans and travelers a bird’s-eye view of Kyoto. You can take that literally, too, as soaring over the city are several of the avian cast members of Ghibli’s most recent theatrical anime, The Boy and the Heron, along with a group of adorable warawara spirits.

▼ Hey guys, I need directions.

The focus of the Ghibli Zen Map, naturally, is temples, with charming hand-drawn versions of, among others, Kiyomizudera, Kinkakuji (a.k.a. the Golden Pavillion), and Tenryuji in the city’s western Arashiyama district. Other points of interest on the map include the Kyocera Museum of Art, Nijo Castle, and Kyoto Station. Another unique aspect of Kyoto’s cityscape is that many of its streets actually have names (a rarity in Japan), and these are labeled on the map as well, either to help you reach your destination or find your way home after indulging in the joy of wandering on a whim across Japan’s cultural capital.

Also conspicuously marked on the map are a number of 7-Eleven branches, and the reason for their inclusion goes beyond just Japanese convenience stores being full of useful items for travelers. Since a Ghibli-illustrated map of Kyoto would be very cool to have even if you’re not planning to travel there right away, the Zen Map is actually available at 7-Eleven Japan stores nationwide.

All you have to do is use the self-service Multi-copy Machine inside 7-Eleven branches (which is also used for various ticketing and payment services) and scan the QR code from the Zen and Ghibli website here, pay the 400-yen (US$2.50) fee, and you’ll receive a freshly printed copy of the map.

It’s not clear how long the maps will be available for, but with the Zen and Ghibli exhibition running through December 6, odds are they’ll be printable at least until then.

title: Japan’s bean sprout shortage hitting Jiro-style ramen businesses hard
description: Could this spell doom for one of the most beloved ramen styles? Bean sprouts, known as “moyashi” in Japanese, make an excellent addition to several dishes with their delightful texture and pleasantly mild flavor. It’s kind of like the Ichiro of the topping world, in that it’s a consistently clutch player that crucially supports a […]
content:
Could this spell doom for one of the most beloved ramen styles?

Bean sprouts, known as “moyashi” in Japanese, make an excellent addition to several dishes with their delightful texture and pleasantly mild flavor. It’s kind of like the Ichiro of the topping world, in that it’s a consistently clutch player that crucially supports a meal, even if it doesn’t stand out too often. And one dish which has embraced the joys of bean sprouts wholeheartedly is ramen.

We’re talking about “Jiro-style ramen” to be exact, a genre of ramen in which almost absurdly high piles of bean sprouts are sometimes placed atop the bowl.

▼ Other toppings are also included, but bean sprouts play a major role.

Jiro-style ramen has built up a cult-like following over the years, to the point people are willing to keep eating it even when the restaurant is on fire. This is thanks in no small part to the noble bean sprout.

This year, however, cracks in the bean sprout supply chain began to emerge. Saiki Shokuhin, a major producer of bean sprouts in the Kanto region around Tokyo, has apparently suspended operations without warning since last June and now appears to be completely shut down.

Many other Jiro-style ramen restaurants have been posting about the dire bean sprout situation on social media as well. Some owners have had to scour local supermarkets in search of bean sprouts in an effort to keep their loyal customers happy, because Jiro-style ramen without a giant pile of bean sprouts is, well… just ramen.

This crisis seems to have been a long time coming. From 2009 to 2026, the number of bean sprout producers in Japan fell from 235 to 86. Among their other positive traits, these immature plants are also known to be extremely cheap, with packs selling for well under 100 yen (US$0.63). The rapid inflation of recent years and even more recent issues with fuel have pushed some producers to the breaking point.

▼ This pack cost Mr. Sato just 28 yen, making it a great addition to any home senbero.

It would seem the only solution is to raise the price of bean sprouts, which would in turn raise the price of Jiro-style ramen, yet another sector desperately struggling to keep their relatively low prices that make them such attractive dining options. If ramen shops raise their prices, then their often cash-strapped customers will also dry up in a lose-lose situation.

In fact, this bean sprout situation is a pretty good illustration of critical flaws in Japan’s economy. Online comments of the news did a surprisingly good job of laying out a lot of the factors behind it.

“The reason bean sprouts were so cheap was the stable production behind them. Disrupt that, and it doesn’t just affect restaurants but households as well.”
“If we want to ensure bean sprouts remain affordably available to everyone, we have to fix the economic factors supporting production.”
“For now, the price needs to go up to keep producers going, but this price instability is unsustainable and needs to change.”
“I always look forward to Jiro-style ramen on my cheat day, and appreciate how affordable they are. But this news gives me pause. Cheap food is great, but if the producers don’t get enough money then the customer will ultimately suffer.”
“I’ve seen packs of bean sprouts for 19 yen at the supermarket and always wondered how they stay in business. I’m grateful that they keep prices so low, but they should charge enough to be sustainable.”
“They’re so cheap already, they’d still be cheap even if the price went up.”
“I used to be a producer wholesaler and supermarket buyers would refuse any kind of price increase, threatening to change producers if we did. This problem is caused by short-sighted buyers who force the producers to shoulder the cost increases until they go bankrupt.”

To summarize, bean sprout producers are dealing with mounting costs for just about everything from fertilizer to fuel. On the other end of the chain, most consumers are struggling with the cost of just about everything rising and have to pay close attention to what they buy and eat. Knowing this, supermarkets and other retailers do as much as they can to keep their prices low and keep their customers coming, including putting pressure on producers not to raise their prices.

It’s easy to see how this system is unsustainable, and poised to break down in spectacular fashion as producers go under, and the supply simply dries up to the point bean sprout prices skyrocket way beyond what they would have had the price just gone up slightly to begin with.

▼ Image this costing 1,000 yen… I might still eat it sometimes.

The comments also showed how many consumers can tolerate price increases when required, but with retailers mainly calling the shots with regard to pricing, it still doesn’t happen. A few years ago, the makers of Garigari-kun ice candy and Umaibo puffed corn snacks made headlines for issuing public apologies for raising their prices by a few yen. Both were met with praise from customers who said they’d remain loyal to companies who are honest about their prices and explain their situation.

Though, in light of recent events, I’m starting to wonder if that could even be a way for producers to go over the heads of retailers and appeal directly to the public. If the bean sprout growers’ association issued a public apology for having to raise prices by 5 yen a pack, they’d almost surely get a good response from people in Japan, leaving buyers with little leverage to refuse said price increase.

Anything’s possible, but ultimately, there are clearly far more fundamental issues with Japan’s economy that need to be worked out so everyone can eat well and make a living. This is just the tip of the pile of bean sprouts on a bowl of Jiro-style ramen.

title: Studio Ghibli adds new Totoro and Jiji blanket socks to its merchandise store in Japan
description: Beloved anime movie characters are perfectly placed for wiggle-toe animation.  The cosy season has finally arrived in Japan, and here to herald its arrival is Studio Ghibli, with a duo of brand new blanket socks. Designed for homey nights in, these warm blanket socks will cuddle your feet and warm your heart, with Totoro and […]
content:
Beloved anime movie characters are perfectly placed for wiggle-toe animation. 

The cosy season has finally arrived in Japan, and here to herald its arrival is Studio Ghibli, with a duo of brand new blanket socks. Designed for homey nights in, these warm blanket socks will cuddle your feet and warm your heart, with Totoro and Jiji serving as our cuddle buddies.

Totoro brings forest charm to this green pair, in calming hues that conjure up the nature-filled home in which he dwells.

Surrounded by forest motifs and his beloved acorns, Totoro sits right above the toe section, so you can bring him to life by wiggling your toes.

Adding to the beauty of the socks is their length, which brings the design, and the warmth, right up your calf. This means you can style them in a number of ways, stretching them out fully to enjoy the forest scene, or letting them bunch up loosely around your ankles, giving you the “loose socks” look once favoured by schoolgirls in Japan.

Fans of Kiki’s Delivery Service will want to slip into the Kiki’s Delivery Service Blanket Socks, which come in a navy colourway.

Waiting for your wiggle-toe animation is black cat Jiji, whose wide-eyed facial expression adds to the magic.

Jiji is surrounded by tulips, recalling the countryside setting of Kiki’s home, and the flower-filled workspace of Kiki’s mother, Kokorin. What looks like brown crosses within the design are actually said to represent pretzels, in honour of the bakery where Kiki works.

Again, the long length lets you fully enjoy the design, or you can let them loose to let the colours shine.

Socks these cute make an ideal gift for Ghibli lovers, but then again, they’re so adorable, we won’t be able to resist buying them for ourselves. Made from a poly-cotton blend, both pairs come in one size, to fit 22-26 centimetre (9-11 inch) feet, and they can be purchased at Donguri Kyowakoku stores and online (links below) while stocks last.

title: Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest Christmas celebration coming to Yokohama next month
description: A Christmas Slime appears, with a Chocobo buddy too! With the winter holiday season on the way, it won’t be long until Christmas decorations start appearing in Japan. Every year the Landmark Plaza and Mark Is entertainment complexes in Yokohama, half an hour south of downtown Tokyo, put up lights and trees, often with some […]
content:
A Christmas Slime appears, with a Chocobo buddy too!

With the winter holiday season on the way, it won’t be long until Christmas decorations start appearing in Japan. Every year the Landmark Plaza and Mark Is entertainment complexes in Yokohama, half an hour south of downtown Tokyo, put up lights and trees, often with some sort of additional theme, and this year that theme is Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest!

The Yokohama Minato Mirai Winter Holiday 2026-Dragon Quest x Final Fantasy Interwoven Winter Fantasy event has a very long name, but it matches that verbosity with a whole lot of cuteness thanks to the mascot monsters of the two iconic video game franchises, Dragon Quest’s Slime and Final Fantasy’s Chocobo. The pair will be appearing at special Christmas tree displays in the central atriums of Landmark Plaza and Mark Is, which are situated across the street from each other in Yokohama’s bayside Minato Mirai neighborhood.

Scattered throughout the two buildings will also be a number of Dragon Quest Slime and Final Fantasy art panels and photo backdrops featuring more members of their beloved bestiaries, with the event’s key art illustration promising the presence of Final Fantasy’s Moogle. There’ll also be a stamp rally where you can earn a free sticker by filling in the blanks on a sheet of paper using stamps near the displays, much like what Landmark Plaza and Mark Is did for their Pokémon Sleep collaboration earlier this year.

Should you work up an appetite on your stamp rally quest, Landmark Plaza will also be hosting the Slichoco (Slime and Chocobo) Kitchen popup cafe in its Cafe Fan Base event space.

In addition to themed food and drinks, customers who order select menu items will receive one of seven exclusive art coasters, showing the creature cast of the Square Enix series frolicking around Yokohama sightseeing spots such as Minato Mirai, the Akarenga red brick warehouse, and Yokohama Chinatown while bundled up in winter attire.

▼ Is that a Final Fantasy Meteor mint chocolate dessert? Because if it is, I’m definitely eating it.

▼ The healing potion-style mocktail’s presentation is pretty slick too.

The Fat Chocobo Curry doesn’t appear to be on the menu, but diners at the cafe will also receive a clear file…

…and for those looking to get their hands on the special merch even if they’re not hungry, Mark Is will also have two popup shops for the collaboration with the customary assortment of key holders, T-shirts, figures, and plushies.

Rounding out the festivities will be an ironing-beads craft workshop in the Cafe Fan Base event area where you can make your own Slime or Chocobo buddy…

…and hologram stickers being given out to shoppers and diners who spend more than 2,000 yen (US$12.60) at select shops and restaurants within Landmark Plaza and Mark Is.

Yokohama Minato Mirai Winter Holiday 2026-Dragon Quest x Final Fantasy Interwoven Winter Fantasy kicks off on November 11 and runs until January 11. Note that the stamp rally, though, wraps up a little earlier, on December 27, so that’s one more reason to go see this Slime and Chocobo as soon as possible.

title: KFC Japan releases its first thigh-meat fried chicken burger in 43 years, but was it worth the wait?
description: It’s been a looooong time since you could get a thigh-meat sandwich at KFC Japan, and now you can get six. A lot of time has passed between now and 1983. To illustrate just how much, 1983 was the year Nintendo’s Famicom (which would become known as the NES overseas) went on sale. In the […]
content:
It’s been a looooong time since you could get a thigh-meat sandwich at KFC Japan, and now you can get six.

A lot of time has passed between now and 1983. To illustrate just how much, 1983 was the year Nintendo’s Famicom (which would become known as the NES overseas) went on sale. In the years since, Nintendo has had time to release a whole slew of other video game consoles, culminating with the launch of the Switch 2 last year.

If you had been one of those early adopters who went out and bought a Famicom in 1983, on your way home from the store you could have swung by KFC Japan and picked up a fried chicken sandwich made with thigh meat. You wouldn’t have been able to repeat that meal choice for the launch of Nintendo’s Super Famicom (a.k.a. Super NES) in 1990, though. Ditto for the release of the Nintendo 64 in 1996…and for every console after that too. Why? Because 1983 was the last time KFC Japan had thigh-meat sandwiches, after which they switched to breast meat.

On October 14, though, KFC Japan released its first thigh-meat sandwiches in 43 years, with the debut of the brand-new Original Chicken Burger series.

There’s a total of six sandwiches in the two-tiered lineup. In addition to the standard Original Chicken Burger, there’s also a Cheese, Teriyaki, and spicy Red-hot version. Those in a more luxurious mood can opt for the Premier Burger, which adds a slice of thick-cut bacon, or the Premier Cheese Burger, providing both bacon and cheese.

This return of thigh-meat chicken sandwiches is such a big deal for the chain that KFC Japan has temporarily rebranded its branch in Tokyo’s Ebisu neighborhood as KFB (“Kentucky Fried Burgers”).

With the new items going on sale on October 14, we dispatched our Japanese-language reporter P.K. Sanjun for some taste-testing. P.K,’s stomach was not quite up to the challenge of eating six fried chicken sandwiches in one sitting, but neither would his pride allow him to settle for just one, so he ordered two to try, the Original Chicken Burger (490 yen [US$3.19]) and the Premier Burger (750 yen).

P.K. started with the Original Chicken Burger, and he was instantly impressed.

The meat was juicy and flavorful, and the characteristic touch of springiness to the texture made him very glad that thigh meat was finally back. There wasn’t a hint of tough dryness to be found as he happily chewed.

The breading for the chicken is very similar to what you get with KFC’s Original Recipe chicken, so P.K. had no complaints there either. The sandwich’s sauce has a bit of tanginess to it, but it serves as an accent, and the star of the show is the delicious chicken. This is a very well put-together fried chicken burger, and more importantly, a very delicious one too.

Moving on to the Premier Burger, the visuals tell you right away that this is a more decadent meal.

The chicken and bun are the same as in the less-expensive Original Chicken Burger, but in addition to the bacon, the Premier Burger also boasts its own unique garlic pepper mayonnaise spread.

Once again, it’s a very enjoyable combination of flavors…but P.K. feels like there’s a little too much going on here. The garlic pepper mayo is pretty insistent about making its presence felt, and the bacon is even more so. As a matter of fact, the bacon dominates the end of the flavor profile, more or less erasing the pleasurable lingering taste of the chicken that P.K. enjoyed with the Original Chicken Burger.

That’s not to say that the Premier Burger is a bad sandwich, and P.K. might have fallen more in love with it if there were no Original Chicken Burger to compare it to. Even though they’re both tasty sandwiches, though, for P.K.’s money, the more straightforward Original Chicken Burger is the way to go, especially since it lets him save 260 yen that he can put towards another Original Chicken Burger the next time he gets hungry.

title: We hunt for treasure at an all-you-can-stuff Kanagawa secondhand shop for just 1,000 yen
description: From kimono to kitchenware, character goods to cleaning sponges, can we fill a basket and get our money’s worth? Secondhand shops can sometimes appear to look like mounds of junk, but to the intrepid explorer, a careful perusal can occasionally turn up some hidden gems. For our Japanese-language reporter Takuya Inaba, secondhand shops have become […]
content:
From kimono to kitchenware, character goods to cleaning sponges, can we fill a basket and get our money’s worth?

Secondhand shops can sometimes appear to look like mounds of junk, but to the intrepid explorer, a careful perusal can occasionally turn up some hidden gems. For our Japanese-language reporter Takuya Inaba, secondhand shops have become something of a hobby, such that whenever he has free time, he enjoys meandering down to a store and combing through their inventory, almost as if he is on a little treasure hunt. He loves the rush of dopamine that floods his brain whenever he finds something remarkable. So, when Takuya heard about a shop in Fujisawa, Kanagawa Prfecture, where you can buy almost everything in the store using a tsumehodai (“stuff-in-as-much-as-you-can”) system, he caught the whiff of a good deal, and decided to head out immediately.

About a 15-minute walk from Zengyo Station on the Odakyu Enoshima Line, the shop is located in a section of a shopping facility called Zengyo Danchi Market.

Its name is Tsumehodai no Mise Recycle Gallery (Stuff-Filling Shop: Recycle Gallery).

According to the explanation written inside, the price varies depending on the volume of items you put into the basket, and even if you pack the basket to the brim, it still only costs 1,000 yen (US$6.30), so it’s reasonably cheap.

▼ Up to the blue level it’s 250 yen, the gray 500 yen, and the pink 750 yen.

According to the clerk, any items with price tags are excluded, but everything else is up for grabs. Plus, the basket is quite large, so you’ll be looking at taking home a fair few items.

▼ Takuya’s adventure begins!

▼ “No way… the sheer amount of things is insane!”

Doing a quick visual check, only a very small fraction of the items have price tags, so Takuya reckoned that about 90 percent of the store was eligible for stuffing in baskets, and he couldn’t wait to dig through everything to see what he unearthed.

The first thing that caught Takuya’s eye was the massive amount of tableware. A little unexpectedly, there was a good selection of items in beautiful condition that, if washed, should be usable without any problems.

On the opposite side to them, there was a wide variety of handy items like notebooks, envelopes, cleaning supplies, and various electronics and charging cords.

He stumbled across some unused sponges and tawashi (traditional Japanese scrubbing brushes), which seemed like they could genuinely be useful too.

There was even unopened aluminum foil and cooking paper. Thinking that these could be a pretty good deal, Takuya popped them in his basket.

Exploring further, Takuya found a large drawer labeled as tsumehodai, which was giving off some treasure vibes, so he opened it and…

▼“Used… pens?”

▼“Who would even want them?”

However, thinking that “a deal is a deal,” Takuya took some just for the fun of it.

Heading over to the space on the other side of the store, Takuya came across a ridiculously well-stocked area filled with clothing.

Being mostly women’s clothes, Takuya declined to make a purchase, but the condition of them looked pretty good.

Takuya even discovered some kimono, which are items that can get pretty expensive, so there might be some really valuable items mixed in there, too.

There were also many nice-looking shoulder bags.

Further back, Takuya also discovered some books.

Takuya decided that he’ll throw a book into the basket that looks like it’ll improve his English conversation skills.

What really got Takuya hyped up, though, were the DVDs. Despite there being a sign saying that they were 100 yen each, the shop staff said that it was fine to include them in the tsumehodai deal, and so Takuyha did.

It was with this mindset that Takuya got overly absorbed in the treasure hunting and had soon filled up his basket.

So, now it’s time to review all the great finds Takuya came across, and to figure out whether it was worth the money or not.

First, an unused donabe (clay cooking pot) measuring 18 centimeters (7.1 inches) across. With these pots probably costing close to 1,000 yen if bought normally, Takuya already felt like he had got his money’s worth just from this.

Next, the aluminum foil and cooking sheets, which are always handy to have.

Takuya also grabbed a mug and bento box set, completely unused, featuring SoftBank’s popular mascot character, “Oto-san” (Dad).

Then, a handkerchief with a picture of Suiteki-kun, the mascot for Tokyo Waterworks that even has its own song. Takuya found it quite cute, so he’s pretty happy he picked it up.

▼ Suiteki-kun’s theme song

After that, there were two DVDs: Speed Racer and Scooby-Doo, both of which were without scratches and played without a hitch.

Takuya also found a Little Bobdog coloring book and brought it home. Little Bobdog was a character originally created in 1988 for the confectionery company Orion.

Seeing his happy little face again brought back some nostalgic feelings for Takuya. It’s these types of items that make him fall in love with secondhand shops all over again.

Adding on to that, there were also some small items like pens and toothbrushes for cleaning, making for a total of 16 items acquired. For Takuya, he felt that getting all of this for just 1,000 yen was a fantastic deal.

▼ The pens actually worked… surprisingly well.

One thing to remember though, is that all goods purchased are non-refundable, so double-check your chosen items before making your payment.

However, Takuya is convinced that if he were to explore the inside of the store even more thoroughly, he might discover some insanely rare gems hidden away, so another visit may well be on the cards in the future.

Searching through items for ones that genuinely catch your interest from among the enormously piled-up goods was a thrilling experience for him, so why not pull out a 1,000 yen bill and go and try it out for yourself?

title: Man in Japan says monkey threw his cat into a pond before attacking him
description: Yamaguchi primate decides to pick fights with two other species. content:
Yamaguchi primate decides to pick fights with two other species.

After several months of bears dominating reports of startling wildlife encounters in Japan, it seems as though the nation’s monkeys have decided to take that notoriety as a challenge. We’ve recently been talking about the dreaded Troop T1, a group of monkeys that’s been running amuck in the town of Yugawara in Kanagawa Prefecture, where they recently surrounded and attacked a man who was out for a morning stroll on the city streets. Now comes an incident on the opposite side of the country, in Yamaguchi Prefecture, where a monkey not only attacked a man, but also reportedly decided to maybe drown a cat.

The man in question is a 49-year-old resident of the town of Shunan. He isn’t necessarily a pet owner, but he says there’s a stray cat that’s made its home in his garden, which has a pond. While the man was at home on Tuesday, at around 3:40 in the afternoon, he heard the sound of a loud splash coming from the pond, which he says was caused when a monkey came into the garden and threw the cat into the water.

While the man was rescuing the cat, the monkey, an adult roughly 50 centimeters (19.7 inches) in height, scampered up onto his roof and stared down menacingly at him. It then jumped back down to ground level, and when he turned away from it, leapt onto his back and clawed at him, leaving long scratches on his skin through the thick work clothes he was wearing.

The monkey then ran off, and the cat seems to have survived the encounter without suffering any severe injuries.

The Tokuyama neighborhood of Shunan, where the man lives, isn’t a major urban area, but it’s far from undeveloped countryside, and his home borders a fairly sizable road.

▼ The approximate area where the incident took place

This isn’t the only startling monkey incident the town has had recently, either. On September 8, in a separate part of Shunan, a monkey grabbed and tore the clothing of a local woman. Police have been stepping up patrols in the area and calling on residents to be cautious. Experts warn that should anyone run into a wild monkey, they should avoid provoking the animal, and also avoid making eye contact (as monkeys can perceive that as threatening behavior) while calmly leaving the area.

Source: Television Yamaguchi Broadcasting Systems via Yahoo! Japan News via Itai News, KRY Yamaguchi Hoso
